purpose: Ketorolac is a strong pain reliever used for short-term treatment of moderate to severe pain, such as pain after surgery or an injury. It also helps reduce inflammation and fever. It is usually used when stronger pain relief is needed but doctors want to avoid opioid (narcotic) pain medicines.
how_it_works: Your body makes certain chemicals called prostaglandins when you are hurt or sick, and these chemicals cause pain, swelling, and fever. Ketorolac works by blocking the enzymes (COX-1 and COX-2) that your body uses to make those chemicals. By reducing prostaglandins, ketorolac helps ease pain and inflammation without being a narcotic.
common_side_effects: Upset stomach, nausea, or indigestion are the most common side effects. You may also notice headache, dizziness, or drowsiness. Some people experience stomach pain or diarrhea. Taking it with food can help reduce stomach discomfort.
warnings: This medication should only be used for a short time — usually no more than 5 days — because longer use raises the risk of serious stomach bleeding, ulcers, and kidney problems. It can increase the risk of heart attack or stroke, especially with longer use or in people who already have heart disease. Avoid ketorolac if you are pregnant (especially in the last 3 months), allergic to aspirin or other NSAIDs, or if you have kidney problems or active stomach ulcers. Always tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, since ketorolac can interact with blood thinners and other NSAIDs.
typical_dosing: For adults, the usual dose by mouth (tablet) is 10 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed, with a maximum of 40 mg per day. By injection (given in a clinic or hospital), it is typically 15 to 30 mg per dose. No matter how it is given, ketorolac should not be used for more than 5 days total. Your doctor will choose the right dose and form for your specific situation.
